archetype.name: Fringe Contender (pass-and-takeaways)
archetype.definition: A Packers team efficient enough on a per-play basis to belong in the playoff race, but one that leans on Jordan Love's arm and a ball-hawking secondary to cover for a broken run game and a fourth-place spot in a stacked division.

report.headline: Efficient enough to contend, but a one-armed offense has a hard ceiling
report.take:
Green Bay is a passing team with a takeaway defense, and not much in between. Jordan Love has started every game and thrown for 2,838 yards. The offense ranks ninth in pass EPA and dead last in rush EPA, so the plan is simple: throw to Matthew Golden, Christian Watson and Tucker Kraft, and let a secondary that rarely gives up explosive passes take the ball away. It works often enough that the Packers rank seventh in net EPA. That is a better underlying profile than their scoring margin shows.

The record and the scoreboard tell slightly different stories. Green Bay is 6-4 having outscored opponents by only 5 points all year, which implies about 4.7 wins. The extra win comes from going 0.75 in one-score games and a turnover margin that ranks third. None of that is fake. LaFleur's Packers have finished positive in turnover margin in most recent seasons, and the defense genuinely ranks fifth in pass EPA allowed. But the margins are thin. The good version of this team showed up in the middle of the season against Chicago, Carolina and New England, when Love's passing EPA reached double digits and the defense piled up multi-takeaway games. The bad version came against Minnesota's top-ranked defense, twice: 39 points allowed in the opener, then a 10-30 home loss with 8 sacks and 4 turnovers.

The numbers hide how fragile both halves are. The run game is broken before the backs get the ball. Yards before contact rank 31st and stuff rate 28th, so this is a line problem, not just the fact that Josh Jacobs has played only three games. On defense, 26 sacks (third) have come from a pressure rate that ranks only 20th. Sacks and takeaways at that pace usually cool off. Behind them is a unit that ranks 26th in red-zone touchdowns allowed and 21st on third down. Add special teams and penalties that both rank 26th, and a lot of hidden yardage leaks away.

From here, the Packers are fourth in a division where Chicago and Detroit are 8-2 and Minnesota is 7-3, so the realistic target is a wild card. The schedule is split. New Orleans, Miami and Houston are games they should win. Buffalo, at Chicago, Detroit and this trip to the Rams are games where the run game's absence and a shorthanded interior line get tested. A 9- or 10-win team is the likeliest outcome, and whether that is enough will depend on whether the turnover luck holds.

strengths.title: Love's passing carries everything
strengths.body: The passing game ranks ninth in EPA, and the staff leans into it with a pass rate over expected that ranks tenth. When the protection holds, the ceiling is high, as in the 45-27 win at New England. The line has been better in pass protection than in run blocking, with a sack rate that ranks eighth over the season. That makes this the most sustainable part of the offense, as long as Love isn't forced into obvious passing downs every series.

strengths.title: Pass defense that takes the ball
strengths.body: Green Bay ranks fifth in pass EPA allowed and third in explosive pass rate allowed, and only one team has more takeaways. Quarterbacks have to work underneath and drive the length of the field, and long drives create chances for mistakes. The coverage looks real, a sharp turnaround from 2025's 22nd-ranked defense. The takeaway pace is the part likeliest to slow.

strengths.title: Efficiency outruns the point margin
strengths.body: The scoring margin is close to even, but net EPA ranks seventh. That points to a team that has played better per snap than its scoreboard shows, though the two Minnesota blowouts do skew the totals. The turnover margin ranks third, and recent LaFleur teams have tended to keep a positive margin, so some of this is a repeatable trait rather than pure luck.

concerns.title: A run game that starts behind
concerns.body: Green Bay ranks last in rush EPA, and the line is a big part of why: backs average 1.72 yards before contact (31st) and get stuffed a quarter of the time. That is why Lloyd and Kaleb Johnson have both struggled while Jacobs has been out, and why the offense ranks 29th in success rate despite a good passing game. With guard Sean Rhyan out, it is unlikely to get better soon.

concerns.title: Sacks and takeaways outrun the pressure
concerns.body: Twenty-six sacks rank third, but the pressure rate ranks only 20th. That gap usually closes, and Micah Parsons hasn't played a snap to help close it. Once offenses get close, the defense bends badly: it ranks 26th in red-zone touchdown rate allowed and 21st on third down. If the takeaways slow down, more of those drives will finish in the end zone.

concerns.title: Hidden yards leak away
concerns.body: Special teams rank 26th in EPA per game, and the team ranks 26th in penalties per game, including 98- and 133-yard flag days in the first two weeks. For a team whose wins come by thin margins, that is the difference between going 0.75 in close games and going 0.50. Penalties have been cleaner lately; the kicking units haven't shown the same improvement.

trend.note: A rough start included blowout losses to Minnesota and Atlanta. Then came a strong middle stretch where Love's passing EPA spiked and the only loss was by three in Detroit. The latest game was a 10-30 home loss to Minnesota with 8 sacks and 4 turnovers, a reminder of how badly this offense breaks when it can't run and can't protect.

nextGame.headline: Short underdog against a better Rams team missing its weapons
nextGame.body:
The Rams have the better profile, fifth in net EPA and fourth in defensive EPA allowed. They have also been less lucky than their record, with negative wins over expected and a 0.4 mark in one-score games. Their defense is built to beat exactly this Packers offense: second in rush EPA allowed and third in deep-pass EPA allowed. The way through is underneath and quick. The Rams rank 27th in pressure rate and 31st in QB-hit rate, and slot and third receivers have produced well above their norms against them. On the other side, a Rams offense that passes far more than expected (second) runs into the Packers' strongest unit, the pass defense. The Book has LAR -2.5 with a 43.5 total, indoors.

Availability tilts things back toward Green Bay. The Rams are without Puka Nacua and Davante Adams, both on IR, and McVay has ruled out guard Steve Avila. Center Coleman Shelton is also out, which strips two interior starters from a line that has been the league's best at preventing pressure. Myles Garrett is questionable after missing Monday's practice, and safety Kam Curl is questionable too. For Green Bay, Jacobs and guard Sean Rhyan are out. Right tackle Travis Glover, an every-snap starter, is questionable. Linebacker Zaire Franklin is listed out, though LaFleur said Monday the team hadn't decided on him for Wednesday. Isaiah McDuffie is questionable. Parsons remains out, which changes nothing from what this defense has been all year.

waysToWin.title: Squeeze a Rams offense missing weapons
waysToWin.body: Without Nacua and Adams, and with two interior linemen out, Stafford is working with a thinned-out passing game behind a patched middle. Green Bay's pass defense ranks fifth in EPA allowed and rarely gives up chunk plays, so the Rams may have to drive the length of the field again and again. That is the setting where this defense has collected its sacks and takeaways.

waysToWin.title: Win the turnover battle
waysToWin.body: Green Bay ranks third in turnover margin per game; the Rams rank 23rd. The Rams' defense has only 10 takeaways. If Love plays clean, the hidden edge goes to the Packers. Their wins this year have mostly come with a takeaway advantage.

waysToWin.title: Quick throws against a soft rush
waysToWin.body: The Rams rank 27th in pressure rate, which gives a shorthanded Packers line a chance to hold up, especially if Garrett sits. Their weak spot in coverage has been third receivers, who rank dead last in production over their own norms against them. Spreading the ball beyond Golden and Kraft, rather than forcing it deep into a top-three deep defense, is the efficient path.

waysToLose.title: One-dimensional again, like Minnesota
waysToLose.body: The Packers' last-ranked run game faces the league's second-best rush defense by EPA. If early downs keep losing yards, Love ends up in obvious passing downs behind a line missing Rhyan and maybe Glover. That is exactly how the 10-30 loss to Minnesota unfolded, with 8 sacks and 4 turnovers. A Garrett return would make this the most likely way the game goes wrong.

waysToLose.title: Rams run and own the clock
waysToLose.body: The Rams' line ranks first in stuff rate and fourth in yards per carry, while Green Bay is middle of the pack against the run and may be without Franklin. Atlanta ran for 242 yards on this defense. Even with the Rams' interior line patched, a steady ground game would shorten the game and keep the Packers' pass rush from getting its chances.

waysToLose.title: Red-zone mismatch decides it
waysToLose.body: Green Bay gives up touchdowns on 69 percent of red-zone trips (26th), while the Rams hold opponents to 43.3 percent (sixth). In a game with a total in the low 40s, settling for field goals while giving up sevens is enough to lose on its own.

nextGame.watch: Green Bay's patched right side and interior line on second-and-long: if Love stays upright against a Rams rush that rarely gets home, the Packers' pass game travels; if this turns into another Minnesota, it doesn't.

restOfSeason.body:
The passing game and the coverage are real and should keep Green Bay competitive every week. The run game is a structural problem that a Jacobs return would only partly fix. Expect the sack and takeaway pace to drift down, given the middling pressure rate, and with it some of the cushion in close games. The red-zone defense and special teams are steady weaknesses, not noise.

The remaining schedule splits cleanly: New Orleans, Miami and Houston are winnable, while Buffalo, at Chicago, Detroit and this game at the Rams are coin flips or worse. Even at nine or ten wins, they'll probably need help from the division logjam to reach the playoffs.
swingFactors: Offensive line health (Rhyan, Glover) and Jacobs' return
Results vs BUF, at CHI and DET

confidence.note: Ten games, clear efficiency signals, but heavy injury churn on both lines and a turnover-driven margin.
